takeaway: Anticoagulate AF when estimated annual thromboembolic risk is at least 2% (CHA2DS2-VASc at least 2 in men or 3 in women); anticoagulation is reasonable at 1% to under 2% [1].
clinicalQuestion: Who with atrial fibrillation should receive anticoagulation to prevent stroke?
background: The 2023 multisociety guideline updates stroke-prevention advice from the 2014 guideline and 2019 focused update [1].
studyDesign: Clinical practice guideline with class of recommendation and level of evidence.
comparator: No anticoagulation, stratified by estimated annual risk.
primaryOutcome: Prevention of stroke and systemic thromboembolism.
mainFindings: Class 1, level A: anticoagulation is recommended when estimated annual thromboembolic risk is at least 2% per year, for example CHA2DS2-VASc of at least 2 in men and at least 3 in women. Class 2a, level A: anticoagulation is reasonable when risk is at least 1% but under 2% per year, equivalent to a score of 1 in men and 2 in women [1].
clinicalMeaning: The decision is risk-based. A score that maps to 2% or more per year is a recommendation, not a suggestion [1].
limitations: The extracted recommendation uses annual risk, with CHA2DS2-VASc as the example. Other modifiers in the full guideline are not repeated here [1].
bottomLine: Recommend anticoagulation at CHA2DS2-VASc of 2 or more in men and 3 or more in women; consider it at 1 in men and 2 in women [1].
practiceImplication: Do not use one threshold for both sexes [1].
trustRationale: Current ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline recommendation with Class 1, Level A evidence for the higher-risk group.
whatNotToOverclaim: Do not apply the Class 1 recommendation to a man with a score of 1.
An AF-burden consensus statement is not this anticoagulation recommendation.
